Prathama Krishi Systems: The First Hundred Retailers

Darbhanga, Bihar — 28 September 2026

1. Opening

Chandan Mishra read the message from Singapore twice before he set his phone down. It was seven in the morning in Darbhanga, and outside his office window the shutters of Laheriasarai Chowk's seed and fertiliser shops were already rattling open for the day. Varsha Das, who sat on Prathama Krishi Systems' small advisory board from Singapore, wanted a number for the next investor update: "Can we say we crossed 100 active retailers before the board call on the 16th?" Chandan had exactly seventeen days — until 15 October, the date by which North Bihar's seed and fertiliser retailers traditionally finish restocking before the Rabi sowing rush makes them too busy to learn anything new. As of that morning, sixty-three shops were using Prathama's inventory and advisory app closely enough to count as activated. He had to decide, by the end of the week, how the remaining seventeen days of the sprint would be spent — and whether the number 100 was even the right thing to chase.

2. Company background

Prathama Krishi Systems was founded in 2024 by Chandan, a former area sales manager for a fertiliser distributor, to solve a problem he had watched for a decade: the small seed, fertiliser and pesticide retail shops that supply Bihar's farmers ran almost entirely on paper ledgers and memory. A shopkeeper in Muzaffarpur might stock forty SKUs across DAP, urea, hybrid maize seed and pesticide brands from Coromandel, IFFCO, UPL and Bayer, yet have no way to know which batch was expiring, which SKU was moving, or what to recommend when a farmer asked why his wheat leaves were yellowing. Prathama's app gave the shop owner a phone-based inventory ledger, GST-ready billing, and a simple agronomy advisory chatbot built on crop-stage and soil data for the districts it served. It charged ₹299 a month once a shop was active, undercutting the free-but-thin tools bundled by large distributors and positioning itself between hyperlocal paper ledgers and the enterprise ambitions of players like DeHaat and AgroStar, both of which worked mainly through their own franchised centres rather than existing independent retailers. Prathama's entire addressable market in its home territory — Darbhanga, Muzaffarpur and Samastipur districts — was the roughly 4,800 licensed agri-input shops shown in Exhibit 1's footnote, and the company's whole strategy rested on becoming indispensable to a meaningful slice of them before a larger player noticed the gap.

3. The situation

For four months, Prathama's approach to acquisition had been entirely by hand. Jahnavi Thakur, who led product and field operations from Darbhanga, ran a two-person field team that walked into shops, sat with the owner through a full day's billing, and only left once the owner had logged a real batch of stock. Of 380 shops visited this way, 190 sat through a full demonstration, 114 installed the app and logged a first batch, and 57 were still using it after thirty days — the bar Prathama used internally for "activated." Three weeks earlier, under pressure to move faster, Jahnavi had tried something different: she paid a large agri-input distributor ₹40,000 to blast its retailer WhatsApp list and host one group demonstration at a Samastipur mandi, reaching 200 shops at once. Forty installed the app; six were still active after thirty days. Poonam Karn, Prathama's data and engineering lead working out of Bengaluru, had since pulled the retention numbers further: of those six distributor-sourced shops, only two were still logging inventory by day sixty — a wisp-thin 2 of 6, or roughly 33%, against a far stickier pattern among the door-to-door cohort. The comparison sat starkly in front of Chandan: one channel was slow and expensive per shop visited, but converted and stuck; the other was fast and cheap to reach, but the users it produced barely used the product at all.

4. The people

  • Chandan Mishra — Founder and CEO, Darbhanga. Spends two days a week himself sitting with shopkeepers, believes trust in Bihar's tight retailer network travels shop to shop faster than any advertisement, and worries that a wave of unhappy, half-used accounts would do Prathama more harm than good.
  • Jahnavi Thakur — Head of Product and Field Operations, based between Darbhanga and Muzaffarpur. Has already interviewed three former agricultural-extension workers she could hire within days, and argues the field method works — it just needs more hands before the sowing window closes.
  • Poonam Karn — Data and Engineering Lead, Bengaluru. Built the dashboard that surfaced the day-60 retention gap between channels; wants any scaling decision to be judged on activated users who stay, not on installs.
  • Varsha Das — Advisory-board member and former operations lead at a Southeast Asian agritech marketplace, Singapore. Needs a credible growth number for the 16 October board call ahead of Prathama's Series A conversation, and favours whichever path gets closest to 100 fastest.

6. The options

  • Option A — Scale the field team. Hire three more agents (five in all) for the sprint, each covering about four shop visits a day over roughly fifteen working days: 300 visits. Applying the door-to-door channel's own visited-to-activated rate of 15% (57 of 380) yields 45 new activations, taking the total to 108 — past the 100 mark. Incremental cost: ₹18,000 per agent for the sprint, ₹54,000 in all, or about ₹1,200 per new activated shop. Upside: preserves the channel that Exhibit 2 shows is both cheaper and stickier per activated shop. Cost: three new hires must be recruited, trained and made productive inside a week, and Jahnavi alone cannot supervise five people across three districts without strain.
  • Option B — Scale the distributor partnership. The distributor's retailer network across the three districts covers roughly 1,000 shops, of which 200 were reached in the pilot; take the remaining 800. At the pilot's own rates — 20% trial starts, 15% of those activated — that is 160 trial starts and 24 new activations, for a total of 87, short of 100. Cost: a flat partnership fee of ₹1,20,000, or ₹5,000 per new activated shop — more than four times Option A's cost per activation — and, per Poonam's day-60 numbers, a channel whose users are far more likely to stop logging inventory within two months. Upside: needs no hiring and can start the same day.
  • Option C — Run self-hosted haat demo camps. Chandan and Jahnavi host four group demonstrations at weekly agricultural markets, reaching about 150 shops each, 600 in all, at the same bulk-outreach conversion rates as the distributor pilot: 120 trial starts, 18 new activations, total 81. Cost: about ₹5,000 a camp for tent, signage and refreshments, ₹20,000 in all — cheapest of the three — but it pulls Chandan away from the anchor shops he personally mentors, and produces the same shallow, low-retention users as Option B.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. What does Exhibit 1 reveal about the real difference between the two channels Prathama has already tested — is it reach, or is it something else?
  2. Whose definition of "success" is Chandan actually being asked to satisfy on 15 October — Varsha's, the shopkeepers', or his own?
  3. If Prathama chooses Option A and still falls short of 100 activated shops by the deadline, has the sprint failed? What would you look at instead of the headline number?
  4. What would you tell Jahnavi about how to keep five field agents' quality of onboarding as high as two agents' has been?

8. A note for the learner

This topic's lesson — do things that don't scale — is not an argument against growth; it is an argument about sequence. Paul Graham's original point, and the reason it belongs at the start of a go-to-market module, is that a company's first users are won by founders doing unscalable, high-touch work that later becomes a repeatable playbook, not by borrowing someone else's scale before you know what makes a user stay. Exhibit 1 and Exhibit 2 together make the underlying mechanism visible: the door-to-door channel converts trial starts to thirty-day activation at more than three times the distributor channel's rate, and costs less than half as much per activated shop even before counting Poonam's day-60 retention finding. A well-reasoned answer treats "100 activated retailers" as a proxy for the real goal — a base of shops that keep using Prathama through the Rabi season and tell other shopkeepers to — not as the goal itself.

On that reading, Option A is the defensible path. It is the only option projected to clear 100 by 15 October, it costs the least per activated shop of any option that reaches the target, and it extends rather than abandons the channel the data says works. Its risk is real — five field agents are harder to manage well than two — but it is an execution risk Jahnavi can plan against, whereas Options B and C carry a channel risk the pilot has already demonstrated: shops that arrive without hands-on onboarding mostly do not stay. Chandan's honest answer to Varsha should not be a bigger number bought cheaply; it should be a smaller, truer one, defended with the retention data behind it — the number a board should actually want to see before a Series A.

Your First 100 Users

Why the founders who win a market are, for a few months, willing to do things that will never work again once the market is won.
Reading time ~14 minutes · Builds on: Early adopters and the chasm

On the second Tuesday of March 2023, Rohan Mehta sat in a one-room office above a stationery shop in Jaipur's Bapu Bazaar with a spreadsheet titled Devika_launch_list.xlsx open on his laptop and forty-one thousand rupees left in the company's current account. Devika Books, the bookkeeping application he and his co-founder Ananya Sood had spent eleven months building for small retail shop owners, had been live for six weeks. It had ninety-four registered accounts and, by the metric that actually mattered, eleven active users — shopkeepers who had opened the app and recorded a sale in the last seven days. Devika Books was not short of a good product. It was short of proof that a hundred strangers, unrelated to Rohan and Ananya by friendship or family, would use it on their own money and their own time, week after week. Investors read that number as the market's verdict before any pitch deck. Rohan's decision that Tuesday was not about a feature or a price. It was about how the next hundred users would be found, and how much of it he was willing to do by hand.

The stakes were specific and dated. The seed round Devika Books was raising closed in ten weeks. The lead investor, a Bengaluru-based fund that had backed two other vertical SaaS companies selling into Indian small retail, had told Rohan plainly that a hundred genuinely active shopkeepers, gathered without paid advertising, was the threshold below which they would not proceed — not because the number itself was magic, but because it was the smallest sample size from which a fund could infer that the product solved a real problem rather than a favour granted to a founder's friends. Rohan had forty-one thousand rupees, a co-founder, one part-time intern, and roughly seventy days.

What "your first 100 users" actually means

The idea has a precise shape once it is separated from its folklore. Your first 100 users refers to the earliest cohort of genuinely independent customers — people with no personal obligation to the founders — who adopt a new product primarily because the founders sought them out, recruited them, and served them individually, using methods that cannot be repeated at the volumes the company will eventually need. The idea was named and popularised by the Silicon Valley investor and essayist Paul Graham in a 2013 piece for his startup accelerator, Y Combinator, titled "Do Things That Don't Scale," though the practice long predates the essay: door-to-door insurance agents and early mail-order catalogue sellers were doing a version of it a century earlier. Graham's contribution was to name the pattern and argue, against the instinct of engineers who want to build a machine that runs without them, that in a company's first months the founders themselves are the growth engine, and that trying to automate acquisition before the company knows who its customer is and why that customer buys is a way of building a beautifully efficient pipe to nowhere.

The sentence Rohan could say in a fundraising meeting without sounding glib is this: "We don't yet have a channel; we have a hundred people we recruited by hand, and the fact that we had to do it by hand is what taught us what the channel should be." The number itself is a convention, not a law of nature — some investors and operators use fifty, others use two hundred — but a hundred survives as the common benchmark because it is large enough to rule out coincidence (eleven happy users can all be lucky; a hundred, spread across independent circumstances, are unlikely to be) and small enough that a founder can still know each one's name, business, and reason for buying.

"Your first 100 users" is not a marketing milestone. It is the manual, unscalable phase in which the founders trade their own time for information about who the product is for — information that later becomes the channel, the pricing, and the onboarding flow that will serve user 10,000.

The mechanics, step by step

The process practitioners actually run, once stripped of its improvisational appearance, has six steps, and Rohan and Ananya's next ten weeks followed all of them, in order, whether or not they had named the steps in advance.

First, narrow the target to a profile so specific it feels uncomfortably small. "Small retailers in India" describes forty million businesses and is useless as a targeting instruction. Rohan and Ananya narrowed it, after the six weeks of slow signups, to "a saree or garment shop owner in one of three specific Jaipur markets, with one or two staff, who currently records daily sales in a paper ledger or a WhatsApp voice note to himself." That description fit perhaps six hundred shops within walking distance of their office — a population small enough to enumerate by hand, which was the point.

Second, build the list yourself rather than buying it. Devika Books did not purchase a database of retailer phone numbers. Ananya and the intern, Kabir, spent four days walking Johari Bazaar, Chandpole, and Tripolia Bazaar, writing down shop names, owner names, and phone numbers obtained by simply asking, in a paper notebook that Kabir digitised each evening. This step, most founders later admit, is the one they were most tempted to skip, and skipping it is the single most common reason a "first 100 users" campaign never gets off the ground: a purchased list contains strangers who cannot place why they are being contacted; a hand-built list contains people the founders have already stood in front of.

Third, reach out personally, and expect most of it to fail. Rohan called or visited every name on the list himself for the first three weeks. This step is where the "doesn't scale" part becomes visceral: a founder capable of building software instead spends entire days on phone calls and shop visits, at a rate of contact that no venture-scale company could sustain past a few hundred people.

Fourth, onboard as a concierge, not as a self-serve product. When a shop owner agreed to try Devika Books, Rohan or Ananya did not send a signup link and wish them luck. They sat with the owner, in the shop, and entered that day's sales into the app themselves, on the owner's phone, while the owner watched. This is the step most often left implicit in retellings of the "first 100 users" story, and it is frequently the difference between a signup and an active user.

Fifth, treat every conversation as a research interview, not just a sales call. Rohan kept a second spreadsheet, separate from the launch list, logging every objection and every feature request verbatim. Sixth, ask for the next name before leaving. Every satisfied visit ended with the same question — "Which other shop owner here would want this?" — because referral inside a tightly bounded geography is, practitioners find, dramatically cheaper than any other channel at this stage, and it tests something a cold list cannot: whether users like the product enough to spend their own credibility recommending it.

The arithmetic: two passes through the funnel

Rohan's first serious attempt, run over the two weeks after that March Tuesday, is worth walking through with real numbers, because the story people tell about "hustling for users" tends to skip the part where the first honest attempt falls short.

In the first pass, Rohan and Ananya worked through the 240 shops on their hand-built list. Ninety-six owners, or 40 percent, agreed to a fifteen-minute demo — already a number that startled them, since it meant three of every five people they approached said no outright, mostly citing a lack of time. Of those ninety-six demos, fifty-eight owners, or 60 percent, created an account before the founders left the shop. But when Rohan checked activity thirty days later, only thirty-nine of those fifty-eight, or 67 percent, had entered a sale in the previous seven days. Net: thirty-nine active users out of 240 shops contacted — a 16 percent yield on the whole list, and, critically, short of the hundred they needed, even before accounting for the shops they had not yet reached.

The second pass changed exactly one input. Rohan and Ananya ran the identical 240-shop list, the identical demo script, and got, unsurprisingly, the identical 40 percent demo rate and 60 percent signup rate — ninety-six demos, fifty-eight signups. But this time, instead of leaving each shop once the owner had created an account, Ananya or Kabir sat with the owner for an additional fifteen minutes and entered that day's transactions into the app themselves, narrating each step, before leaving. Thirty days later, forty-nine of the fifty-eight signups, or 85 percent, were still active — not sixty-seven percent this time, but eighty-five. The one changed input, activation rate, moved the net yield from 16 percent to 20 percent of the list, and moved the absolute count of active users from thirty-nine to forty-nine on an identical list of 240 shops. It was, on its own, still short of a hundred. What it proved was cheaper and more valuable than the shortfall: the bottleneck was never demo interest or willingness to sign up. It was the ten minutes of friction between creating an account and typing in the first real entry, and that ten minutes was worth a founder's time to remove by hand. Three more such passes through adjoining market lanes, at a comparable 20 percent net yield, is what eventually carried Devika Books past its hundred, in week nine rather than week two.

Nuances a learner must sit with

It is a phase, not a permanent operating model

The entire value of hand-recruiting users is that it is temporary. A company still personally onboarding user 8,000 the way it onboarded user 8 has usually mistaken a bootstrapping tactic for a strategy, and is quietly bleeding margin it will need later. The discipline is to extract, from every hand-served user, the pattern that will let the next thousand serve themselves.

"First 100 users" is not the same claim as "first 100 signups"

A signup is a click. The number that matters — the number Rohan's investor actually asked about — is users who returned and used the product on a cadence the product's own logic implies: daily for a bookkeeping tool used at point of sale, weekly for a tool used to close monthly accounts. Conflating the two lets a founder celebrate a funnel that never converts.

Representativeness matters more than the count

A hundred users drawn entirely from one founder's college WhatsApp groups tell you that friends will humour a friend; they tell you almost nothing about whether a stranger will pay. The number is only diagnostic when at least a meaningful share of it consists of people with no relationship to the founders beyond the product itself — which is why Devika Books's hundred, drawn from three market lanes the founders had never worked in before, carries more evidential weight than a hundred drawn from a personal network would have.

It applies best where the buyer can be found in physical or identifiable clusters

Devika Books worked because Jaipur's shopkeepers cluster geographically into walkable markets. A product whose buyer is, say, a solitary freelance graphic designer scattered anywhere with an internet connection cannot be "walked" in the same way, and the hand-recruitment channel has to be reinvented as, for instance, personally commenting on relevant online communities rather than knocking on doors. The mechanics generalise; the specific channel does not.

It is routinely confused with a pilot or a beta programme

A beta programme is typically run by the product team on a pre-selected list of friendly accounts to catch bugs. Recruiting the first hundred users is a go-to-market exercise aimed at strangers, run to learn who buys and why, not primarily to find defects. The two are sometimes combined in a small company, but conflating their purposes leads founders to over-trust feedback from an unrepresentative, technically sophisticated beta list.

A hundred satisfied users does not prove the business model works

Devika Books's forty-nine active users in pass two were using the product for free. Their willingness to open the app daily said nothing yet about their willingness to pay ₹499 a month for it, which is a separate and later question the first-100 exercise cannot answer on its own; it can only, at best, tell a founder whom to ask.

Manual recruitment can mask a channel problem instead of solving it

If nine of every ten prospective users on the hand-built list decline even a demo, the founders should ask whether they have simply chosen the wrong market lane rather than concluding they need to visit more shops in the same one. The exercise generates signal about the target profile, not just about outreach volume, and a thoughtful founder revisits the profile itself when the top of the funnel refuses to move.

The number itself deserves scepticism before it is quoted to an investor

A careful newcomer should ask, before repeating "we have a hundred users" in a meeting: active by what definition and over what window; recruited through which channel, and how much of that channel is repeatable; and what fraction have a relationship with the founders that a true stranger would not have. Investors experienced with this genre ask exactly these three questions, and a founder who cannot answer them precisely has not yet done the exercise properly, only performed it.

Consumer, B2B, marketplace — and how the same idea changes with company size

The mechanics above came from a B2B product, and B2B is where the "hundred users" convention sits most comfortably, because B2B buyers are fewer, more identifiable, and more tolerant of a founder showing up in person — Devika Books's shopkeepers, contacted one at a time, are a fair representative case. A consumer product changes the arithmetic without changing the underlying discipline. Consider Darpan Fit, a habit-tracking fitness app whose two founders sourced their first hundred users not from a physical market but from three sources they could still reach individually: their own extended personal networks, a small cluster of Bengaluru college WhatsApp groups, and direct comments left, one at a time, under fitness-related Instagram posts inviting people to try the app and reply with feedback. The channel differs entirely from Devika Books's; the discipline — founders personally present for the first use, personally reading every reply, resisting the urge to buy paid reach before the product's retention curve is understood — is identical.

A marketplace complicates the exercise further because it needs, in effect, two separate hundreds recruited in a particular order. Dhanvi Homes, a fictional service-marketplace connecting households with electricians and plumbers in Pune, could not simply recruit a hundred households and wait; a marketplace with no supply is worthless to the households, and a marketplace with no demand is worthless to the electricians. Dhanvi Homes's founders instead recruited twenty electricians by hand first, personally guaranteed each of them a minimum number of paid jobs in the first month by finding those jobs themselves — sometimes posting the jobs on their own household's behalf — and only once the supply side had a credible base did they begin recruiting households, so a new household's very first request would find someone available. The "first 100 users" idea, for a marketplace, is really a sequencing problem: which hundred first, and how to fake the far side of the market convincingly enough, by hand, that the real side of the market has a good first experience.

Company stage matters as much as product category. Everything above describes a company with no existing customer base, no sales motion, and no brand recognition to lean on. Inside a large, established company — a bank launching a new lending product, a retailer launching a loyalty programme — the analogous exercise is usually called a pilot or a controlled rollout rather than "the first hundred users," and it differs in two important ways: the company already has a base of existing customers it can invite selectively, which removes the coldest and hardest part of outreach, and it faces a different risk, cannibalising or confusing an existing product line, that a founder recruiting strangers from zero does not face. The instinct to do things by hand still applies — a product manager inside a large bank piloting a new product with fifty branch relationship managers, sitting with them individually to watch how they actually use it, is doing a corporate-scale version of what Rohan did in Johari Bazaar — but the surrounding constraints, and the definition of what counts as a meaningful early cohort, change with the size of the organisation running the exercise.

Common mistakes

Automating outreach before understanding who responds

The symptom is a founder who has sent a mail-merge campaign to eight hundred prospects and can quote an open rate but cannot describe, in a sentence, what a single respondent's business looks like. The underlying misunderstanding is treating volume of contact as a substitute for depth of understanding, when at this stage the two trade off directly against each other. The cheapest diagnostic: ask the founder to describe, unprompted, the last three people who declined and why; if they cannot, the outreach has already become impersonal enough to have lost its purpose.

Counting signups instead of return usage

The symptom is a dashboard proudly showing "127 users" next to a usage chart that is flat or falling. The underlying misunderstanding, as noted above, is conflating account creation with adoption. The cheapest diagnostic is a single query: what fraction of registered accounts took the product's core action in the last seven days, and has anyone actually run that query before the number was quoted in a meeting.

Building a bespoke feature for every early user's request

The symptom is a product roadmap that has become a list of one-off favours, each traceable to a specific early user's specific complaint, with no visible pattern connecting them. The underlying misunderstanding is treating every piece of feedback from a hand-recruited user as equally load-bearing, rather than watching for the same request surfacing independently across several unrelated users before committing engineering time to it. The cheapest diagnostic is a shared, dated log of every request, reviewed weekly for repeats, which is exactly the second spreadsheet Rohan kept beside his launch list.

Waiting for the product to feel finished before recruiting anyone

The symptom is a team six months past its planned launch date, still refining a feature no user has asked to see, having spoken to zero prospective customers in that period. The underlying misunderstanding is believing that hand-recruitment requires a polished product, when the entire logic of concierge onboarding — a founder sitting beside the user, filling gaps by hand — means the product can be rougher than it will ever be allowed to be again. The cheapest diagnostic is to ask whether outreach could begin this week using the product exactly as it stands today, manual patches and all; if the honest answer is yes, the delay is a choice, not a necessity.

What good looks like

By week nine, Devika Books had crossed 104 active users across the three original market lanes, using the concierge method from pass two on subsequent batches of shops. What made the effort recognisably good, rather than merely persistent, was not the raw hours logged but three specific habits. First, Rohan and Ananya could each independently list every active user's shop name and the one detail that had almost stopped them from adopting the product, because they had personally onboarded most of the hundred and had treated the objection log as seriously as the signup count. Second, they had already begun to see a pattern in the requests — eleven shop owners, unprompted, had asked whether Devika Books could generate a simple end-of-day GST summary for their accountant — and had resisted building it until the twelfth and thirteenth request confirmed it was not idiosyncratic. Third, and most tellingly, seventeen of the 104 active users had arrived through a referral from an existing user rather than through direct founder outreach, which was the first faint evidence that the product could eventually acquire users through a mechanism other than the founders' own legwork — the earliest sign of the channel that pass one and pass two had been designed to discover.

What Rohan decided

Rohan did not solve the problem by hiring a sales team, which was the option the intern had suggested and which the remaining thirty-eight thousand rupees in the account could not in any case have supported. He decided, that Tuesday, to have Ananya and Kabir spend the next eight weeks doing nothing but the concierge pass through adjoining Jaipur market lanes, in person, with no advertising spend and no attempt to build a signup funnel that could run without them. The reasoning traced directly back to what the topic this page builds on had already established: the earliest adopters of a genuinely new product are not a random sample of the eventual market, and they will not simply arrive on their own, which is exactly why finding them requires the founders' own hands rather than a channel budget. The decision cost Devika Books two months it did not obviously have to spare, and it produced, by week nine, both the hundred active users the seed round required and a request pattern — the GST summary — specific enough to become the product's next roadmap priority with evidence behind it rather than a guess.

What Rohan needed to learn next, once the hundred were secured, was how to tell which of those hundred were worth building for at volume and which were an unrepresentative pocket he had gotten lucky with — the discipline of activation and retention metrics that turns a hand-counted cohort into a defensible growth model. Two questions are worth sitting with before moving there. First: in your own product, what is the one thing you would be willing to do by hand for a stranger this week that you know you could not keep doing for the ten-thousandth customer — and have you actually done it yet, or only planned to? Second: if someone asked you, the way Rohan's investor asked him, exactly how your current users were found and what fraction of them owe you nothing personally, could you answer in specifics, or only in the rounded, comfortable language of a slide?

Your First 100 Users

Hand-recruiting the first cohort is not a hustle story. It is a sampling decision, a capital-allocation decision and a measurement decision taken simultaneously, usually by people who have not noticed they are taking all three.
Reading time ~28 minutes · Builds on: Early adopters and the chasm · Learning objective: do things that don't scale

1Two decisions, eleven days apart

On Thursday 8 August 2024, in a rented unit on the second floor of an industrial estate off Pune's Mumbai–Bengaluru highway, Sandhya Iyer laid three purchase requisitions side by side on a desk and did not sign any of them. Iyer had spent eleven years as an instrumentation engineer with a Pune auto-components supplier before co-founding Kaveri Instruments with Devraj Naik in early 2023. Their product, Kaveri Trace, was a battery-powered temperature and door-open logger with an embedded SIM, bolted inside the cargo box of a refrigerated vehicle or on the wall of a milk chilling centre, feeding a dashboard and a WhatsApp alert whenever a load drifted out of range. The device had cleared its third field revision. The landed cost per unit, including enclosure, calibration and the certification overhead, was ₹5,100 at a 250-unit production run; connectivity ran ₹85 per device per month. Kaveri Instruments had ₹31 lakh of cash and, by Naik's calculation, about twenty-six weeks before the arithmetic stopped working.

The three requisitions represented three theories of the next ten weeks. The first was for 100 units, to be placed free with any cold-chain operator who would accept them: capital outlay ₹5.1 lakh plus ₹1.02 lakh of first-year connectivity. The second was for 45 units, placed at a ₹2,500 commissioning fee and ₹350 a month, half the intended price. The third was for 30 units at the full ₹6,500 plus ₹700 a month, sold as a product rather than seeded as an experiment. Iyer's seed investors, a Mumbai fund that had backed two industrial-IoT companies, had used the phrase "a hundred devices in the field" in three consecutive board updates. What Iyer could not decide was whether a hundred devices placed free would tell her anything she would still believe in December, or whether thirty devices that someone had actually paid for would tell her more, on a sample too small to say almost anything with confidence.

Eleven days later and 1,400 kilometres north, on Monday 2 September, Vikram Salve of Kartikeya Systems faced a decision that looked like the opposite of Iyer's and was in fact the same decision wearing different clothes. Kartikeya Systems, founded in Gurugram in 2023 by Salve — fourteen years in credit risk at a large non-banking financial company — and Sheetal Nadar, sold an AI assistant that ingested bank statements, GST returns and bureau reports for a small-business loan application and drafted a first-cut credit memo for a human analyst to check, correct and sign. On the morning of 2 September the product had 118 registered users who had each opened at least twenty files in the previous thirty days. By any ordinary reading, Kartikeya Systems had cleared the hundred-user mark comfortably, and Nadar had already drafted the slide.

Salve had spent the weekend with the account breakdown and had arrived at an uncomfortable position. Of the 118 analysts, 74 sat in a single central underwriting hub in Chennai belonging to one NBFC client; 22 sat in a Jaipur-headquartered lender; 14 and 8 in two fintech lending platforms. Four customers. One of them was the source of nearly two-thirds of all usage, and that customer's chief credit officer was an old colleague of Salve's. The question Salve put to Nadar on Monday morning was not whether they had a hundred users. They plainly did. It was whether they had a hundred observations, and whether a fund's diligence team, or more importantly Salve himself, should treat 118 seats inside four accounts as evidence of anything beyond the fact that four buying decisions had gone their way.

These two decisions organise everything that follows. Iyer's problem is that the first hundred costs capital she may not recover and may not be able to interpret. Salve's problem is that he can report a hundred users truthfully and learn nothing from them. Both are versions of a single question that the standard advice — go find a hundred users by hand — systematically hides: what exactly is the first hundred a sample of, and what is it powerful enough to prove?

2The idea, its history, and the schools that disagree about it

Begin with a definition precise enough to argue with. The first hundred users are the earliest cohort of adopters recruited individually by the founding team, by methods deliberately chosen for their information yield rather than their cost-efficiency, during the period in which the company does not yet know which acquisition channel, which customer profile and which activation sequence will eventually work. The cohort exists to convert three unknowns — who buys, why they keep using it, and what has to happen between signup and habit — into stated, falsifiable claims. The number is a convention. The definition's load-bearing clause is "methods chosen for information yield", because that clause is what separates hand-recruitment from a small, cheap, badly designed marketing campaign.

The practice is older than its name. Direct-selling organisations, mail-order catalogue houses and insurance agencies were doing versions of it in the nineteenth century; the industrial instrumentation business Iyer came from has run "place a unit at a friendly plant and sit with the maintenance engineer" trials for as long as anyone can remember. What changed in the 2000s was the rise of software companies whose founders were engineers by temperament, who instinctively reached for a system when confronted with a problem, and who therefore needed to be argued out of building an acquisition machine before they knew what it was supposed to acquire. Steve Blank's customer development method, set out in The Four Steps to the Epiphany in 2005, made the first formal case: a startup is not a small company executing a plan but an organisation searching for a business model, and the earliest customers — Blank's "earlyvangelists" — exist to falsify hypotheses, not to make the quarter. Paul Graham's 2013 essay "Do Things That Don't Scale", written for Y Combinator founders, gave the practice its popular vocabulary and its canonical illustrations: Airbnb's founders going door to door in New York to photograph listings, Stripe's founders installing their own product on a prospect's laptop during the conversation that sold it. Eric Ries supplied the experimental framing, Sean Ellis supplied a measurement instrument in the form of the "how would you feel if you could no longer use this product" survey, and by the late 2010s "do things that don't scale" had hardened into something close to received wisdom.

Received wisdom is precisely where an experienced practitioner should slow down. There are at least five distinct positions in circulation, they are routinely blended into a mush that none of their authors would sign, and the differences between them decide what Iyer and Salve should actually do this quarter.

The founder-concierge school

Would sign: in the first months the founders are the acquisition channel and the onboarding flow, and the manual work is the mechanism by which the company learns what to automate. Would not sign: that this is a permanent operating model, or that manual recruitment is itself evidence of demand. Graham's essay is explicit that the point is recruitment plus insatiable attention to the users recruited, and that the practice has an expiry date.

The customer-development school

Would sign: the first cohort's purpose is hypothesis falsification; a cohort that cannot falsify anything is wasted regardless of its size. Would not sign: that the cohort should be optimised for retention or revenue. Blank's practitioners are content to end the exercise with a hundred users and a killed hypothesis, which founders and their investors experience as failure and which Blank regards as the cheapest possible outcome.

The channel-first growth school

Would sign: a cohort acquired by means that cannot be repeated teaches you about the product but nothing about the business, and the company must find product–channel fit, not merely product–market fit. This is the position associated with Brian Balfour's market–product–channel–model framing and with Andrew Chen's observation that acquisition channels decay. Its adherents would not sign the proposition that any hundred users will do; they insist the first hundred be recruited through at least one candidate channel so that the cost, the conversion and the selection bias are measurable and transferable.

The enterprise design-partner school

Would sign: where the buying unit is an organisation, the unit of learning is the account, not the user, and five properly instrumented design partners beat a hundred seats. Would not sign: the seat count as a milestone at all. Practitioners in this tradition — the sales-engineering lineage running through Mark Roberge's work on the science of scaling sales — treat the first hundred users as a consumer-internet artefact wrongly imported into B2B.

The measurement school, and the sceptics

Would sign: product–market fit is a signal you detect in a cohort's behaviour, not an achievement you manufacture by attentiveness. Its sharper wing adds a genuine attack: hand-recruitment contaminates the very measurement it is meant to produce, because founder attention inflates activation and retention by an unknown margin. The sceptics go further — the canon of "do things that don't scale" stories is assembled entirely from survivors, and we have no visibility into the thousands of teams who did exactly the same things and died anyway.

The disagreement is not about whether to talk to early users. Everyone agrees on that. The disagreement is about what the first hundred is evidence of — a product worth building, a channel worth scaling, a hypothesis worth killing, or an account worth expanding — and each answer implies a different cohort, recruited differently, at a different cost.

3Mechanics in depth: the arithmetic nobody writes down

Expert practice differs from competent practice less in the steps taken than in the quantities tracked while taking them. Four pieces of arithmetic do most of the work, and three of them are almost never written down.

The founder-hour budget, and why the hundred is a capacity decision

Hand-recruitment consumes a fixed, non-transferable resource: founder hours. Kaveri Instruments could field three people — Iyer, Naik and a field engineer — for roughly 45 usable field hours each per week, or 135 hours weekly. A single Kaveri Trace installation consumed 90 minutes on site, about 70 minutes of travel in a Pune–Ahmednagar radius, and 25 minutes of follow-up, plus a further 1.4 hours of hand-holding in the first week: call it 4.5 hours per activated device. But roughly 40 per cent of field time was spent reaching operators who declined, so the effective cost was closer to 7.5 hours per activated device, and 135 hours a week bought about eighteen. A hundred devices was therefore a five-to-six week programme at full intensity — feasible, but consuming essentially all senior capacity for a quarter.

Kartikeya Systems' arithmetic looked entirely different. Onboarding one credit analyst took about 5.5 hours: two ninety-minute shadow sessions, plus reviewing that analyst's first dozen drafted memos. But before any analyst could log in, the account required an information-security review, a data-processing agreement compliant with India's data-protection regime, and a deployment into the lender's own cloud environment — roughly 40 hours of founder and engineering time per account, irrespective of whether the account then produced five users or seventy-five. The consequence is the single most useful reframing in this topic: the relevant denominator is not hours per user but hours per independent observation. Under an identical 1,000-hour budget, Kaveri Instruments could buy roughly 130 independent observations; Kartikeya Systems, where each account is one observation costing 40 hours of setup plus perhaps 20 hours of seat onboarding, could buy about sixteen.

Effective sample size, and why 118 users can be twelve

Salve's discomfort has a formal name. When observations arrive in clusters — seats inside accounts, subscribers inside a housing complex, drivers inside a fleet — they are correlated: analysts in the same underwriting hub share a manager, a file mix, a training session and a lunch table. The standard correction is the design effect, neff = n / [1 + (m − 1) × ICC], where m is the average cluster size and ICC is the intra-cluster correlation, the share of variance in the outcome attributable to which cluster a user sits in. Kartikeya's 118 users sat in four clusters, m ≈ 29.5. Behavioural outcomes inside a single functional team typically carry an ICC between 0.15 and 0.40; take 0.30 and the arithmetic gives neff = 118 / [1 + 28.5 × 0.30] = 118 / 9.55 ≈ 12. Salve did not have a hundred users in any statistically meaningful sense. He had about a dozen, plus a very good relationship in Chennai.

What a hundred can and cannot detect

Even an uncontaminated hundred is a blunt instrument, and practitioners consistently overestimate it. For a proportion such as week-four retention, the standard error is √[p(1−p)/n]. At p = 0.60 the 95 per cent interval is roughly ±9.6 points at n = 100, ±19 points at n = 25, and ±4.8 points at n = 400. Two consequences follow, and both are load-bearing. First, a hundred users can establish that retention is probably not catastrophic and probably not spectacular, and essentially nothing finer. Second, the moment the cohort is split — by segment, by channel, by pricing arm — the intervals widen so far that the comparison becomes decorative. To distinguish 60 per cent retention from 70 per cent at conventional power requires roughly 350 users per arm. Any founder running a four-way segment comparison on a hundred users is reading noise, and the expert tell is that they quote the point estimates to a decimal place.

The founder premium, and the hold-out nobody runs

The second-order effect that separates careful practitioners from enthusiastic ones is the founder premium: the portion of observed activation and retention caused not by the product but by a named human being who visited, called, fixed things personally and made the user feel obliged. Call it δ. It is never zero. It is frequently larger than the product effect. And it is measurable at trivial cost by holding out an arm — shipping a slice of the cohort with no concierge treatment at all. Iyer had modelled exactly this: courier twenty of the hundred loggers with a printed card and a three-minute video, and install the rest. If installed units activated at 88 per cent and couriered units at 45 per cent, then δ ≈ 43 points, and the honest reading of Kaveri Trace's adoption in August 2024 was that a large fraction of it was a person in a van. That is not a reason to stop installing. It is a reason to know the number, because δ is precisely the quantity that must be engineered down to zero before any channel investment makes sense, and a company that has never measured it will discover its size the first month it tries to grow without founders in the field.

The manual residue ladder

The last piece of arithmetic is the one Graham's essay implies and almost no one instruments: the trajectory of manual effort across the cohort. Expert teams log, for every user, the minutes of unscalable human work consumed, and they watch the slope across quartiles of the hundred. Kaveri's log, by the time Iyer reviewed it in October, read 190 minutes per install for the first twenty-five, 150 for the next twenty-five, 95 for the third and 55 for the fourth — a decaying curve, which is the signature of learning. A flat line across quartiles means the team is performing the ritual of doing things that don't scale without extracting the pattern, and a rising line means the product is absorbing bespoke commitments faster than it is shedding them. The slope, not the level, is the diagnostic.

4When the idea applies, stated as testable claims

5Hard edge cases and what happens at the organisational seams

Two-sided and platform businesses convert the problem from recruitment to sequencing. The binding constraint is not a hundred users but the smallest network that works for its participants without the rest of the network existing — an atomic unit, typically a single geography, campus or trade. Practitioners hand-build the thin side first and then manufacture the other side themselves, which is why the folklore contains so many stories of founders personally fulfilling orders and personally posting listings. The failure mode is peculiar to this case: a marketplace can reach a hundred users on both sides and still have no marketplace, because the hundred are distributed across twenty geographies with two participants each and never transact.

Regulated products break the mechanics at the recruitment step, not the product step. A lending, insurance or medical product frequently cannot be given to a hundred strangers at all: a live credit decision requires a licensed entity, a diagnostic device may require a regulatory clearance, and a payments flow requires approvals that arrive on their own timetable. Teams in this position run a split cohort — a small, fully compliant live group and a larger shadow group using the product on historical or synthetic data — and the discipline is to state plainly which conclusions rest on which group. Salve's team, it is worth noting, could recruit a hundred analysts to run Kartikeya against last year's closed files without touching a live credit decision, and that is a genuine and underused instrument.

Hardware-plus-software is Iyer's world and has an asymmetry that software founders consistently underestimate: the cohort is financed out of capital, not time, and the units do not come back. A hundred loggers in the field is ₹5.1 lakh of cash converted into an experiment, plus a service obligation — failed units must be replaced, batteries replaced, calibration certificates reissued — that persists long after the learning has been extracted. Sophisticated hardware teams therefore run deliberately smaller first cohorts with much heavier instrumentation per unit, accepting wide confidence intervals in exchange for depth, and they write an explicit exit clause into the placement agreement so the experiment can be ended.

AI-native products introduce a genuinely new wrinkle: the first hundred users are simultaneously the first hundred sources of evaluation data, and the product's quality is a function of that data in a way that a conventional product's is not. This creates a virtuous loop and a trap. The loop: every corrected credit memo at Kartikeya was a labelled example, and by 2 September the team had 4,100 analyst-edited memos, an asset no amount of advertising could have bought. The trap: because a human is in the loop, the team can silently supply the missing capability themselves — Salve's engineers had, in the Chennai account's first six weeks, manually written prompt templates for eleven specific loan product types. Whether that is honest concierge work or a disguise for a product that does not exist is a judgement call, and the distinguishing question is whether the manual work is being converted into artefacts the system will later use unaided. There is also a cost asymmetry: unlike a software seat, an AI seat has a real marginal cost, and a hundred hand-recruited free users consuming long-context inference can burn ₹2–4 lakh a month with no revenue attached.

Multi-product companies and organisational seams. Once a company has two products, the first-hundred exercise for the second is corrupted by the existence of the first: the cheapest hundred users are the existing customers, and they will adopt out of relationship, bundling or sheer curiosity, producing an adoption curve that will not reproduce in the open market. Mature companies say they solve this with "pilots". What they generally do is invite a friendly subset of the existing base, measure enthusiastic usage, and ship — and the honest ones then quietly re-run the test on a cold segment before committing a sales quota to it. The most consequential seam, though, is the handover. The first hundred are recruited by founders; user 101 onwards is recruited by a new hire with no equity, no product knowledge and no authority to promise a fix. Conversion rates fall by a third to a half at this transition as a matter of routine, and the teams that survive it are those that treated the founder premium δ as a number to be engineered down during the first hundred rather than a charm to be enjoyed.

6Nine nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

The cohort is a sample, and samples have a design

A competent practitioner asks how many users; an expert asks what the sampling frame was, how candidates were selected from it, and what systematically got excluded. The distinction matters because the first hundred is used to make an inference about a population of millions, and inference from a sample with an undocumented selection rule is not inference at all. The tell in the wild is simple: ask how the hundred were chosen and listen for whether the answer describes a rule ("every chilling centre in three districts with more than 2,000 litres a day") or a history ("we just reached out to whoever we could find"). The obvious reading — that any hundred real users beats zero users — is wrong because a badly designed hundred does not merely fail to inform; it actively misleads, and misleads in a direction the team cannot see.

The founder premium is a number, not a mood

Everyone concedes that founders inflate early results. Experts measure by how much, because δ is the gap between current performance and the performance a channel would deliver, and therefore the true size of the product work remaining. The tell is the absence of any untreated arm anywhere in the company's history: if every single user was personally onboarded, the company has no estimate of what the product does on its own and will discover it, expensively, in the first month of paid acquisition. The obvious reading — that a hold-out wastes users the company cannot spare — is wrong because twenty deliberately under-served users are the cheapest insurance available against a six-month channel investment built on a mis-attributed activation rate.

Activation is a product decision wearing a service costume

The manual steps performed during onboarding are, almost always, a specification for a missing product capability. When Iyer's field engineer physically mounted the logger, aligned the probe and entered the customer's threshold temperatures, he was executing three unwritten requirements. The tell is a team that can describe its concierge onboarding warmly but cannot produce a list of the discrete manual steps with a time cost against each. The obvious reading — that concierge work is relationship-building — is wrong, or at least incomplete: it is requirements-gathering conducted with the hands, and a team that does not transcribe it is paying the cost and discarding the output.

Refusals carry more information than acceptances

The users who said yes are, by construction, unrepresentative of the market; the users who said no are a random-ish sample of everyone else. Expert teams therefore keep a refusal log with as much care as a signup log, coded by reason, and treat a shift in the refusal mix as the earliest available signal that the target profile is wrong. The tell is a founder who can recite the hundred but cannot characterise the two hundred who declined. The obvious reading — that refusals are noise from people who did not get it — is wrong because the single most expensive error at this stage is persisting with a segment that is declining for a structural reason the team has not bothered to name.

Concentration destroys evidence faster than small numbers do

This is Salve's nuance, and it generalises far beyond enterprise seats. Sixty subscribers in one housing society, forty drivers in one fleet, thirty analysts in one hub: in each case the effective sample is a handful, and the correlated circumstance — one lift lobby, one depot manager, one credit policy — is doing work the team will attribute to the product. The tell is a user list that has never been tabulated by parent entity or by location. The obvious reading — that concentrated adoption shows intensity of need — is wrong in a specific way: it shows that one environment supports the product, which is exactly the claim that expansion will test and frequently falsify.

The retention window must match the job's natural frequency

Weekly active usage is a meaningful measure for a bookkeeping tool used at point of sale and a meaningless one for a credit analyst who touches twenty files a month or a distributor who reviews cold-chain excursions when a consignment is disputed. Experts derive the window from the underlying job before they derive any number from the data, and they say out loud what cadence the product's own logic implies. The tell is a dashboard whose default window is seven days for every product the team has ever built. The obvious reading — that a shorter window is more conservative and therefore safer — is wrong; a mismatched window does not understate performance, it randomises it, and randomised metrics get over-interpreted in both directions.

Willingness to pay is a separate experiment that the cohort can poison

A hundred delighted free users establish that the product is useful; they establish nothing about price, and worse, they can foreclose the pricing experiment by anchoring an entire reference community at zero. Experts introduce a price into some portion of the first hundred precisely because the resulting refusals are the most informative refusals available, and because a cohort converted from free to paid a year later converts at rates that bear no relation to a cold segment's. The tell is a board slide that reports a hundred users and an annual revenue figure without stating what fraction of the hundred generates the revenue. The obvious reading — that charging early suppresses adoption and slows learning — is right about adoption and wrong about learning.

The cohort should be built to be fired

The first hundred is a scaffold, and a scaffold left standing becomes a structure. Expert teams write down, in advance, the graduation criterion — the condition under which they will stop hand-recruiting and switch to a channel — and they state it in terms of δ and the manual-residue slope rather than in terms of a user count. The tell is a company at 800 users still routing every new account through a founder's calendar, describing this as "high touch" rather than as unresolved product debt. The obvious reading — that attentiveness is a competitive advantage — is true for as long as the per-user manual minutes are falling and false the moment they plateau.

Watch what users stopped doing, not what they asked for

Feature requests are the least reliable output of the first hundred, because articulate users describe the product they can imagine rather than the behaviour they have changed. The durable signal is substitution: the spreadsheet that stopped being updated, the WhatsApp group that went quiet, the paper register that no longer leaves the drawer. Experts audit for abandoned workflows and treat a request unaccompanied by a substitution as a courtesy rather than a demand. The tell is a product log rich in verbatim requests and empty of any note about what the user used to do instead. The obvious reading — that listening to early users means building what they ask for — is the single most common route from a promising first hundred to an incoherent product.

7How the practice actually differs by product type and company stage

Some of the differences across product categories are real and some are asserted by people selling frameworks; it is worth separating them. Consumer products have cheap observations and expensive attention: a hundred users can be reached in a fortnight, but their retention is dominated by habit formation, so the honest measurement window runs weeks past the point at which the founders want an answer, and the hundred is almost always too small to read the curve that matters. B2B with a small buying unit — one owner, one decision — is the archetype for which the advice was written, and here the standard version applies with minimal adjustment. Enterprise inverts it: the unit is the account, the correct target is five to eight design partners with contractual clarity about what the company gets in return, and a team that chases a hundred seats in that setting is optimising a number that no enterprise buyer, investor or operator treats as meaningful. Marketplaces and platforms replace the count with a density threshold, as discussed. Hardware replaces founder-hours with capital and adds an irreversible service tail. AI products add the evaluation-data loop, a real marginal serving cost, and the specific ambiguity of human-in-the-loop work.

Where the difference is often asserted and is not real: the claim that consumer products can skip hand-recruitment because distribution is digital. The channel differs — personal replies in a community rather than a site visit — but the requirement that a named founder personally observes early users failing to activate does not soften, and consumer teams that skip it typically discover a fatal onboarding step months later at ten times the cost. Equally unreal is the claim that AI products can substitute synthetic evaluation for early users; synthetic data reveals whether the model does what the team imagined, never whether the team imagined the right thing.

Stage changes the exercise in three specific ways. At pre-seed and seed, the hundred is a search instrument and the founders are its only sensors. At Series A, the same activity continues but its purpose shifts from discovery to channel construction — the company is now hand-recruiting through candidate channels in order to price them. Inside a large company, the exercise is real but its politics are different: the cohort is usually available for free from the existing base, which makes it cheap and contaminated, and the internal version of the founder premium is the sponsorship of a senior executive who has told people to use the thing. The tell that distinguishes a genuine corporate pilot from pilot theatre is what happens to usage in the week after the steering-committee review: a real cohort is indifferent to the meeting.

8Three worked examples, including one that failed

Kaveri Instruments: buying two things with the same capital

Iyer's eventual programme, run from mid-August to late October 2024, placed 80 of a 100-unit build. Sixty units went out installed, at a ₹2,500 commissioning fee and ₹350 a month, deliberately spread across three sub-segments — 24 to dairy chilling centres, 20 to pharma and pathology transport, 16 to ice-cream and frozen-food distributors — with no single customer taking more than four units. Twenty units were couriered with a printed card and no site visit, to a randomly chosen slice of the same candidate list. Twenty were held in reserve. The installed arm activated at 88 per cent within seven days; the couriered arm at 45 per cent, giving δ = 43 points with a wide but decisive interval. Ninety-day retention on the installed arm was 79 per cent, on the couriered arm 40 per cent. Revenue over the ten weeks was ₹3.1 lakh against ₹4.1 lakh of capital and ₹68,000 of field cost — a loss, as intended. What Iyer bought with the loss was a measured founder premium, a segment-level retention read showing pharma transport at 92 per cent and ice-cream distribution at 61 per cent, and a manual-residue curve falling from 190 to 55 minutes per install.

Kartikeya Systems: trading revenue for independence

Salve's programme from September to December 2024 deliberately degraded the company's revenue quality in exchange for statistical independence. Rather than expanding within the Chennai hub — where another forty seats were available and would have been the easiest incremental revenue in the company's history — Kartikeya built a self-serve sandbox running on synthetic and historically closed files, requiring no security review and no data-processing agreement, and recruited small lenders and loan-service providers into it at three to eight seats each. By mid-December there were 19 additional organisations, 74 additional seats, and an average revenue per account of ₹41,000 a year against ₹9.6 lakh for the Chennai account. The user count rose from 118 to 192; the effective sample size rose from about 12 to about 46. The team learned two things they could not have learned by expanding in Chennai: that time-to-first-useful-memo was 11 minutes for lenders who used a standard bureau report format and 3 days for those who did not, and that the product's apparent strength on unsecured business loans did not survive contact with loan-against-property files, where analyst edits per memo rose from 4 to 17.

Kalyani Fresh: a hundred that validated a place, not a product

The instructive failure belongs to Kalyani Fresh, a Bengaluru weekly vegetable-box subscription founded by Aparna Kulkarni in 2023. Kalyani Fresh reached a hundred paying subscribers in nineteen days — 63 from two gated communities in Whitefield where the founders and an early employee lived, 24 from an alumni group, 13 from a barter arrangement with a food-focused Instagram account. Week-eight retention was 71 per cent, which Kulkarni reasonably read as strong. In March 2024 the company expanded into three additional pin codes, hired two delivery staff and raised a ₹1.2 crore bridge. Week-eight retention in the new pin codes was 22 per cent.

The post-mortem identified three causes, none of which was visible in the original cohort. Delivery cost per box was ₹18 in the two founding complexes, where forty boxes went to one guard desk in one lift lobby, and ₹96 in the new pin codes, where the same forty boxes meant nineteen stops. Substitutions — the inevitable consequence of a produce business — had been handled personally by Kulkarni over WhatsApp within minutes; at four times the volume they went to a shared inbox and took a day. And the founding cohort's tolerance was social: neighbours do not cancel on neighbours quickly. The recovery took seven months and consisted of redefining the unit of expansion from the pin code to the building with at least twenty-five subscribers, recruiting building by building through a resident champion given three months free, and refusing service to addresses below the density threshold. A relaunched hundred, spread across four complexes, ran at ₹31 a box delivered and 64 per cent week-eight retention. Kalyani Fresh's first hundred had not been a bad cohort; it had been an excellent cohort answering a question the company did not know it was asking.

9Failure modes, their early warning signs and the cost of catching them late

The failures below are not exotic; each one appears in ordinary companies run by capable people, and each has a diagnostic that takes under an hour. What makes them expensive is that every one of them produces, in its early stage, a number that looks like progress.

Table 4 — Six failure modes with their earliest visible sign and the cost of a late catch

Two of these deserve a word beyond the table. The founder-premium failure is the most expensive because its cost lands as a surprise at exactly the moment a company has just raised money and hired a growth team, which is to say at the moment it has the least appetite to hear that its activation rate was partly a person. And the feature-capture failure is the most insidious because it feels, from inside, exactly like the customer obsession the company has been told to practise. The distinguishing question is not how attentively the team listens but whether any mechanism exists for requiring independent corroboration before engineering time is committed.

10Where experts genuinely disagree

Four disagreements in this area are live, in the sense that competent, experienced practitioners hold opposing views and the evidence does not settle them. Presenting them as settled is the single clearest marker of someone who has read about this topic rather than practised it.

Is hand-recruitment causal or merely correlated with success? The affirmative case rests on mechanism rather than data: manual recruitment is the only way to observe activation failure directly, and the canonical successes did it. The negative case is methodologically serious. The evidence base consists entirely of survivors; we cannot see the far larger population of teams who door-knocked with equal devotion and died, and there exist well-known products whose first thousand users arrived through a shared link with no founder contact whatsoever. What would have to be true for the affirmative to be wrong: that products whose early cohorts arrived through self-serve channels survive at comparable rates once one controls for category. Nobody has that dataset, because the denominator is unobservable, and this is unlikely to change.

Should the first cohort pay? The pricing school holds that money is the only unfaked signal and that a free cohort measures politeness. The access school holds that price selects on procurement capability rather than on need — particularly acute in Indian small-business markets, where a genuinely enthusiastic user may still be unable to authorise a recurring payment — and that a free cohort is the only way to observe the product's value independent of the buyer's budget process. Both positions are defensible; the resolution most experienced operators actually adopt is to price some of the cohort rather than all or none, and then to be explicit about which conclusions came from which arm. Iyer's programme is an instance of exactly this compromise.

Must the first hundred come through a candidate channel? The channel-first school says yes: a cohort recruited by means no employee can repeat produces a company that cannot grow. The concierge school says no, and says it with force: insisting on channel repeatability at the search stage prematurely narrows the company to whatever is cheap to reach, which is rarely where the deepest need lives. What would have to be true for the channel-first school to be wrong: that the information gained from unrepeatable recruitment reliably transfers into channel design later. It sometimes does — Iyer's field visits genuinely prefigure a service-partner channel — and sometimes does not, as with a founder's fifteen-year network in credit risk.

Is a hundred the right number at all? The measurement school notes that the most-used product–market-fit instrument requires around a hundred survey responses, which at realistic response rates implies three hundred or more users, and that a hundred-user cohort therefore cannot even run the standard test. The operational school replies that the number's virtue is human, not statistical: a hundred is the largest cohort a founding team can know individually, and the individual knowledge is the point. Both are correct about different things, which is why the sensible practitioner reports the count and the effective sample size and refuses to let either stand alone.

11What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this topic recruits users and reports a count. Someone who has internalised it behaves differently in five observable ways. They state the sampling frame before they start recruiting, and they can produce it as a written list. They maintain a hold-out arm from the first week, on principle, and can quote their own founder premium to within a few points. They report effective sample size alongside headline count without being asked, and visibly discount their own conclusions when the two diverge. They keep the refusal log as carefully as the signup log and can characterise the market's objections in three or four coded categories with rough frequencies. And — the hardest of the five — they write down, in advance, the condition under which they will stop, so that the decision to graduate from hand-recruitment to a channel is made by a criterion rather than by exhaustion or by an investor's question.

There is a sixth marker, subtler than the rest: a master of this practice treats the first hundred as an expense with a defined return rather than an achievement with a defined size. Iyer's ₹4.8 lakh loss bought a measured δ and a segment ranking, and she could say so in a sentence. That sentence — here is what this cohort cost, and here is the specific uncertainty it removed — is the one that a competent practitioner cannot yet produce and an expert produces reflexively.

12What the protagonists decided

Iyer signed a modified version of the second requisition on 13 August 2024. She built a hundred units and committed eighty: sixty installed at half price across three deliberately separated sub-segments with a four-unit cap per customer, twenty couriered unattended as a control arm, twenty held back. Her reasoning was that a hundred free devices would have produced an uninterpretable result at maximum cash cost, and thirty full-price devices would have produced an interpretable result on a sample too small to segment; the middle option bought a readable retention signal, a first estimate of willingness to pay, and — the part her investors had not asked for — a measurement of how much of Kaveri Trace's performance was the product and how much was Devraj Naik in a van. When the ice-cream distribution segment came back at 61 per cent ninety-day retention against 92 per cent in pharma transport, she had the evidence to narrow the company's go-to-market rather than to widen it.

Salve made his decision on 4 September, and it cost Kartikeya Systems money. He stopped reporting 118 users as the headline and began reporting "four production deployments, 118 seats, effective independent sample about twelve" — a formulation his lead investor initially read as weakness and, by the December board meeting, was quoting back to other founders. He declined, for one quarter, the forty easy incremental seats available in Chennai, and instead spent ten weeks building a sandbox on synthetic and closed files that let small lenders try the product without a security review. The average revenue per new account was four per cent of the Chennai account's. The effective sample size roughly quadrupled, and the discovery that analyst edits per memo rose from four to seventeen on loan-against-property files — invisible inside a hub that did not write that product — redirected two engineers for the following quarter.

Discussion questions

1. Iyer spent ₹4.8 lakh, roughly a sixth of her remaining cash, to learn a founder premium of 43 points and a segment ranking. Was the control arm of twenty couriered units worth the twenty installations it displaced — and how would you value that information if you sat on her board?

2. Salve turned down the easiest revenue in his company's history in exchange for statistical independence. Under what conditions would that be the wrong trade, and what would you need to see in the Chennai account's behaviour to reverse the decision?

3. Kalyani Fresh's first hundred were genuine paying strangers-enough customers with 71 per cent retention. Identify the single cheapest test Kulkarni could have run before the March expansion, and say what it would have cost her had it come back negative.

13Going deeper

  1. Early adopters and the chasm. The topic this page builds on, and the one that explains why a hand-recruited hundred is systematically unrepresentative of the mainstream market rather than merely a small slice of it. It unlocks the discipline of treating the transition out of the early cohort as a distinct strategic problem rather than as continued growth.
  2. What a GTM strategy is. The first hundred produces raw material — a segment ranking, a refusal taxonomy, an activation sequence — that is worthless until it is assembled into a stated choice of who, what, how and at what price. This is where Iyer's 92-versus-61 per cent finding becomes a company decision rather than a data point.
  3. Channels: paid, owned, earned. The natural successor question once the founder premium has been measured and engineered down: which channel can carry the acquisition that the founders' hands were substituting for, and at what cost per activated user.
  4. Inbound vs outbound. Hand-recruitment is outbound in its purest and most expensive form. Understanding what inbound requires — and how long it takes to build — explains why the first hundred almost always has to be outbound even for companies whose eventual motion is inbound.
  5. Product-led growth. The end state in which activation happens without a human, which is precisely the state a company reaches by driving δ to zero across the first hundred. Reading this topic against PLG makes clear that concierge onboarding is not the opposite of product-led growth but its research phase.
  6. Sales-led growth. Salve's world. It supplies the vocabulary — design partner, deal, playbook, quota-carrying repeatability — in which the enterprise objection to the hundred-user milestone is properly stated, and it explains what replaces the milestone.
  7. Product-led sales (PQA / PQL). The synthesis of the previous two, and the mechanism by which a company that hand-recruited a hundred small users eventually identifies which of them signal an account worth a salesperson's time — the natural next problem for both Kartikeya's sandbox cohort and Kaveri's placed devices.
