Ankur Campus Networks: Which Hundred?

Rajahmundry, Andhra Pradesh — Sunday, 27 September 2026

1. The night before

The Danavaipeta office was empty except for Mythili Dantuluri and the security guard downstairs, who had twice come up to ask whether to switch off the corridor lights. Three documents had held her for four hours. A renewal form for the state engineering-employability mission, to be filed by 9 October or Ankur Campus Networks would drop out of empanelment and lose twenty-five of its thirty-four paying colleges. A bridge term sheet from Upavan Capital Partners: three crore rupees, half on signature and half on reaching one hundred live colleges by 31 March 2027, lapsing on 12 October. And a memorandum from her data scientist in Toronto, titled simply Who is actually using this.

Ankur's dashboard said 48,000 student accounts and 3,100 active in the last thirty days. Zenia Mantena's memorandum said 1,910 of those 3,100 — about 62 per cent — had ever opened the product on a device belonging to the student rather than to a placement office. The rest of the activity came from shared desktops, almost all of it in colleges Ankur had never visited.

At Monday's leadership call she would have to say what to do with the remaining three months of cash. Her co-founder wanted more field staff; her engineering lead wanted the roadmap back; her employer lead wanted to stop selling to colleges altogether; her investor wanted a hundred colleges. Somewhere in the fourth hour it had occurred to her that each was counting a different hundred, and that she had never made them argue about which hundred mattered.

2. How Ankur got here

Mythili had spent seven years running campus hiring for an IT services firm's Visakhapatnam delivery centre: driving between engineering colleges in the Godavari districts, sitting in placement cells that ran on WhatsApp groups and Excel files, watching good students lose offers because someone had sent the wrong spreadsheet on the wrong day. She and Gayatri Vegesna, a former training-and-placement officer at a Kakinada college, founded Ankur Campus Networks in November 2023 to build the missing layer: a workflow tool for the placement cell, a student profile employers could trust, and offer tracking that produced the statistics colleges need for NAAC accreditation and NIRF submissions without weeks of manual reconciliation.

By August 2024 Upavan Capital Partners had led a seed round of ₹5.40 crore on a simple story: India graduates over a million engineers a year, the AICTE internship mandate had made internships a compliance requirement rather than a nicety, and nobody was serving the tier-two and tier-three colleges where most of those students study. Naukri Campus, Unstop and Internshala were strong with students but thin inside the placement cell.

In March 2025 Ankur made the decision that now defines its options. The state's engineering-employability mission invited vendors to be empanelled, letting colleges licence the software from mission funds rather than their own budgets. Empanelment brought distribution — eighteen colleges in six months, twenty-five by mid-2026 — on three conditions: a reporting module built to the mission's specification, which took two of nine engineers for six months; a price held at ₹1.20 lakh per college per year to March 2028; and no charging of students at an empanelled college. The trade looked obvious: distribution was the hard part, everyone said, and a module nobody else had built would be a moat.

3. The industry

Campus recruitment in India is a seasonal, three-sided market nobody owns end to end. Colleges buy software; students use it or ignore it; employers decide whether any of it was worth the trouble. The large IT services recruiters run their own national qualifier tests and portals, and treat placement software as a file format rather than a product. Job boards reach students directly and have no need of the placement cell. Global capability centres, a new generation of which Andhra Pradesh is courting for Visakhapatnam, hire in small batches and care about screening quality, not volume.

Ankur's sharpest rivals came at the market from opposite ends. Sopaan Career Systems, funded out of Hyderabad, sold top-down to private university groups; on 24 September it announced a sixty-college network signed in one agreement, a number Govind Tammineni forwarded to Mythili within the hour. Nishtha Assessment Labs, whose proctored-testing contracts covered much of the affiliating-university examination load, had begun bundling a placement module free with them; Rozgaar Setu Systems had added a campus tab to its job board, buying student attention with cash-back.

Two regulatory facts pressed on the product. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 makes a student's marks and contact details personal data, and Ankur's largest source of accounts — placement officers uploading a whole batch as a spreadsheet — sits least comfortably with a notice-and-consent regime. And the mission now required the same module from all four empanelled vendors, so Ankur's six engineer-months had bought a licence to compete, not an advantage.

4. What happened, and what turned out to be wrong

The internal narrative shifted three times. Through 2025 the company believed it was winning: eighteen empanelled colleges live by September and a board slide reading "34,000 students onboarded." Nobody asked where those students had come from. In March 2026 the module shipped two quarters late, pushing the student application's redesign into a backlog Mareike Vogt in Berlin had stopped updating out of embarrassment. In June, with growth flat, Gayatri stopped managing the field team remotely and went into colleges herself.

What she did was deliberately unscalable: two days in each placement cell, a resume workshop run in person, a full drive sat through beside the placement officer, and no departure until a real employer had interviewed a real shortlist through the product. Between 2 June and 25 September she did this at nine colleges across Rajahmundry, Kakinada and Eluru — seventeen weeks, a rate of roughly 2.3 colleges a month. Those nine are the source of almost everything the company can point to: 9,480 of the 48,000 accounts, 2,260 of the 3,100 active students, and 148 of the 170 offers — 87 per cent. Exhibit 1 sets the two channels side by side.

In August, Gayatri screened 210 student profiles by hand to build a shortlist of thirty-one for Beej Fluid Systems, a Kakinada pump-and-valve maker hiring its first intern cohort. Beej interviewed fourteen and made eleven offers at the end of the internship — just under 79 per cent, a figure Murali Gorantla has put on the first slide of every employer deck since. It cost about forty-six hours of a founder's time, four hours per hire.

Then, on 18 September, Zenia's instrumentation — live only since 12 August, so covering five weeks — produced Exhibit 5, and the headline number changed meaning. Among the twenty-five empanelled colleges, 690 of the 840 students counted as active had only ever appeared on a placement-cell desktop and a further ninety on a lab machine in a timetabled slot. Sixty students across twenty-five colleges had opened Ankur on a phone of their own. The company had spent eighteen months believing it had a distribution advantage and a usage problem; it now looked as though it had neither, only colleges that had bought software and a much smaller set of students who had adopted a product.

5. The people

Mythili Dantuluri, Founder and Chief Executive, Rajahmundry. Believes the nine founder-led colleges are the only real evidence the company has, and has told nobody she is no longer sure the college is the customer. She signed the empanelment and would have to explain reversing it.

  • Gayatri Vegesna — Co-founder, Campus Operations, Kakinada. Position: the field method works and needs eight more people. Incentive: the campus organisation is hers. Not saying: she cannot describe what she does in a form another person could repeat, and two of the nine colleges have asked when she is coming back.
  • Fanindra Peddada — Engineering, Bengaluru. Position: renewal means eighteen more months of mission reporting and no student app. Incentive: two of his nine engineers interviewed elsewhere this quarter. Not saying: the slow first-load on entry-level handsets is his doing, not the mission's, and the retention data would look different if it were fixed.
  • Murali Gorantla — Employer Partnerships, Pune. Position: sell hiring outcomes to a hundred firms in the Kakinada–Visakhapatnam corridor and let colleges come free. Incentive: his variable pay rides on employer revenue. Not saying: most of his nineteen posting employers wanted a curated shortlist by email — an agency service Gayatri performs herself.
  • Zenia Mantena — Data Scientist, Toronto. Position: no growth decision should rest on the current activity definition. Incentive: the audit is the most consequential thing she has produced. Not saying: six weeks of device data cannot separate a disengaged student from an engaged one where shared computers are how students use software at all.
  • Malathi Chodavarapu — College Success, Singapore. Position: the empanelled colleges can be revived with structured onboarding. Incentive: their churn is her metric. Not saying: on her own call logs, seventeen of the twenty-five have not spoken to anyone at Ankur in four months.
  • Ghanshyam Adusumilli — Sales, New Jersey. Position: two US-headquartered captives setting up in Visakhapatnam would pay for screened shortlists now. Incentive: an enterprise logo resets his year. Not saying: both want candidates from institutions Ankur does not serve.
  • Govind Tammineni — Partner, Upavan Capital Partners, Mumbai; board observer. Position: a hundred live colleges by March is the only number the next round can be raised on. Incentive: he must carry a mark-up to his own committee. Not saying: his fund's follow-on capacity for this vintage is nearly exhausted.

7. Voices

8. The options as Mythili sees them

  • A. Renew empanelment and chase the hundred. File by 9 October, sign the bridge, and go after the mission's second cohort, expected to empanel forty to fifty-five colleges across four vendors. A proportionate share is twelve; taking a whole forty-college cohort, plus fourteen more from Gayatri's team at 2.3 a month, puts Ankur at eighty-eight by March, not a hundred. It also locks the ₹1.20 lakh price to March 2028 and keeps two engineers on mission reporting.
  • B. Drop empanelment and go deep in the Godavari districts. Lose twenty-five colleges and ₹30.00 lakh of ARR — half the subscription line — and rebuild around the founder-led method at ₹3.40 lakh a college. The second tranche becomes unreachable, so the runway is 6.7 months and no more. From the nine that remain, a hundred colleges would take forty months at the current rate, unless the method can be written down and taught, which nobody has done.
  • C. Flip to employer-first. Sell hiring outcomes to a hundred firms in the Kakinada–Rajahmundry–Visakhapatnam corridor, of which an internal count suggests around 480 employ fifty or more engineers, and treat colleges as free supply. Here the "hundred" is a number the company has never tried for and has seven data points on.
  • D. Take Ghanshyam's retainers. ₹18–22 lakh of screening revenue before December — about half a month of runway — on candidates sourced from colleges Ankur does not serve. Immediate, profitable, and a staffing business wearing a software company's cap table.

Mythili had written the four on the whiteboard and had noticed, after midnight, what was wrong with the list. A counts colleges. C counts employers. B counts neither and hopes for students. D counts rupees. Nowhere was a line saying which hundred users the company was trying to earn, or what it would accept as proof. Exhibit 3 can be read as proving the founder-led channel three times as expensive per college and half as expensive per offer; Exhibit 5 as proving the empanelled colleges dead, or as proving that Ankur never built for how students in those colleges get online.

9. Deadlines and hard constraints

The renewal closes on 9 October and cannot be filed late; the Upavan term sheet lapses on 12 October. Cash is ₹136 lakh against a net burn of ₹42.49 lakh a month: 3.2 months without the bridge, 6.7 with the first tranche. The ₹1.20 lakh price cap and the ban on charging students at empanelled colleges run to March 2028 and survive a renewal. Two of nine engineers stay on mission reporting for as long as Ankur is empanelled. The DPDP Act exposure on batch-uploaded records is unquantified and has never been put to the board. Beej Fluid Systems expects a shortlist for its January cohort by 20 October, and Gayatri alone can produce one. The season peaks in November: whatever is not in motion by mid-October waits until July 2027.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Exhibits 1 and 5 describe the same 3,100 students. Which is the better measure of whether Ankur has users, and what must be true for the other to be right?
  2. Exhibit 3 gives three costs per offer — ₹28,409, ₹1,26,591 and a blended ₹32,794. Who inside the company benefits from each, and which would you put in front of the board?
  3. Gayatri's nine colleges produced 148 of the 170 offers. Is that evidence the method works, or that one person works? How would you tell the difference before committing money to either?
  4. Ankur has three candidate users — placement officer, student, employer — and counts the one that pays. If you had to pick a single hundred to win by March, whose would it be, and what would you stop doing?
  5. The March 2025 empanelment bought distribution at the price of pricing power and engineering capacity. Was it the wrong decision, or a right decision used wrongly? What does your answer imply about renewing on 9 October?
  6. It is Monday morning, 28 September. What does Mythili do first, what does she tell the call, and what does she say to the board about a hundred colleges by March, knowing the bridge is the difference between three months of cash and seven?

At half past one she switched off the corridor lights herself. On the river road the thought that stayed was not the term sheet or the renewal form. It was Zohra Balusu's sentence: your software did not tell us that; she did. Gayatri had been in nine colleges and had made something no dashboard could see. Whether that was a product waiting to be written down, or a person who would eventually stop, was the question Mythili had circled for four hours, and she went home without an answer.
